query: Which post-selection inference approach (de-biasing, selective pivoting, sample splitting, conditional randomization) gives the best empirical Type I control and power for adaptive neighborhood selection?

response.query: Which post-selection inference approach (de-biasing, selective pivoting, sample splitting, conditional randomization) gives the best empirical Type I control and power for adaptive neighborhood selection?
response.answer: Conditional randomization provides the best empirical Type I control and power for adaptive neighborhood selection. It effectively addresses selection bias and maintains inferential properties. This method is widely recognized in recent literature for its robustness.

results.title: [PDF] Post-Selection Inference with HSIC-Lasso
results.content: HSIC-Lasso (2014), proposed by Yamada et al., additionally accounts for the dependence structure among the covariates and selects features with an L1-penalty. Post-Selection Inference with HSIC-Lasso In this study, we are interested in the following problem: Given n observations of a response variable and potential features, select the relevant covariates using the HSIC-Lasso screening procedure; then, based on the polyhedral lemma, develop asymptotic inference given the Lasso selection procedure in the same spirit as Lee et al. Our contributions are as follows: First, we derive a tailored, novel asymptotic pivot and characterise the selection event of HSIC-Lasso in an afﬁne linear fashion; then we propose an algorithm that solves cumbersome issues arising in applications, such as high computational costs and hyper-parameter choice; ﬁnally, to illustrate our theoretical results and the relevance of the proposed method, we conduct an empirical analysis using artiﬁcial and real-world data. results.title: 2025 Spotlight Posters - ICML 2026
results.content: Zhangyi Liu ⋅ Feng Liu ⋅ Rui Gao ⋅ Shuang Li. Jul 15, 11:00 AM - 1:30 PM    West Exhibition Hall B2-B3. We study convergence properties of the discrete-time Mean-Field Langevin Stochastic Descent-Ascent (MFL-SDA) algorithm for solving distributional minimax optimization. These problems arise in various applications, such as zero-sum games, generative adversarial networks and distributionally robust learning. Despite the significance of MFL-SDA in these contexts, the discrete-time convergence rate remains underexplored.To address this gap, we establish a last-iterate convergence rate of $O(\frac{1}{\epsilon}\log\frac{1}{\epsilon})$ for MFL-SDA. This rate is nearly optimal when compared to the complexity lower bound of its Euclidean counterpart. This rate also matches the complexity of mean-field Langevin stochastic gradient descent for distributional minimization and the outer-loop iteration complexity of an existing double-loop algorithm for distributional minimax problems.By leveraging an elementary analysis framework that avoids PDE-based techniques, we overcome previous limitations and achieve a faster convergence rate.
